lesson.menu_title: Owning the Room in Any Language -- Cross-Cultural Executive Communication

lesson.subtitle: Lesson 20 -- Owning the Room in Any Language
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Denise Gadelha Rocha | Lesson 20 -- Owning the Room in Any Language

listenings.text: There is no native speaker in any meeting I chair. My head of claims is Italian, my pricing lead is Colombian, my reinsurance team sits in Poland, and I am Dutch. English belongs to nobody in that room, and the standard is not London or New York. The standard is whether the four of us leave with the same understanding. I have watched people arrive with beautiful, fast, idiomatic English and lose the room in ten minutes, because idiom is exactly what does not survive the crossing. The colleagues who do well slow down by about ten percent, avoid the clever phrase, and say the level of commitment out loud. Not we will look at it, which means four different things in four countries. Something closer to this is a decision, this is an intention, or this is a preference. That habit is worth more than any accent.

For a long time I thought that being clear meant being direct, and I was proud of it. Then I spent two years working with colleagues who never say no, and I discovered that I had been mistaking politeness for agreement, and building plans on it. The sentence that taught me was that would be difficult. I heard hesitation. It was a refusal, delivered exactly as it should have been, and I was the one who could not read it. What changed my results was not becoming indirect. It was learning to ask the second question. When you say difficult, are you telling me it does not work? Written down it looks almost rude, and in practice people are relieved, because you have given them a way to say the thing without losing face. I still choose my own register. I simply stopped assuming that mine is the neutral one.

extra_audio.text: Where do you land on the January date? When you say it would be difficult, are you telling me it does not work? Let me put it in the note as a group issue, not as your objection. Would the first week of February give your team the room it needs?

reading.rtitle: Group Communication Note -- How Decisions Are Voiced Across the Regions
paras: This note is written for leaders whose working English contains no native speakers. Across the group, the same decisions are taken in the same language and voiced in four different ways. None of them is the correct one, and treating the Milan style as the standard has cost us alignment more than once.

In Milan, disagreement is usually voiced as a question, and rank is acknowledged before the point is made. In the northern markets, the point comes first and the acknowledgement is thought unnecessary. Read in the wrong direction, the first sounds evasive and the second sounds blunt. Both are behaving correctly at home.

In the Latin American markets, agreement in the meeting is frequently the polite beginning of a conversation rather than its conclusion, and the real position arrives afterwards, one call at a time. In several Asian markets a proposal is rarely refused outright: that would be difficult is a refusal, and colleagues who have read it as hesitation have gone on to plan around a decision that was never taken.

Regional leaders are therefore asked to state the level of commitment explicitly rather than assume it is heard, and to calibrate rather than translate. Where a message must travel across three regions at once, the middle register is preferred: the point is made, the person is protected, and nothing is left to be inferred. Nobody in this group is required to sound British or American.
reading.source: Internal note -- Group Communications, circulated to regional leadership
